title: Feedforward Networks
Feedforward Networks
text:
1.2 The digits as tensors

Show codeimport numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from torch import nn
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

_ = torch.manual_seed(481)
digits = pd.read_csv("data/optdigits-test.csv", header=None)
x = torch.tensor(digits.iloc[:, :64].to_numpy(), dtype=torch.float32) / 16
y = torch.tensor(digits[64].to_numpy())
n_train = 1200
order = torch.randperm(len(x))
x_train, y_train = x[order[:n_train]], y[order[:n_train]]
x_test, y_test = x[order[n_train:]], y[order[n_train:]]
n_test = len(x_test)
print(x_train.shape, x_test.shape)

torch.Size([1200, 64]) torch.Size([597, 64])


The exercises use the 1,797 handwritten digits from the course overview, from the same local copy, data/optdigits-test.csv, of the UCI Machine Learning Repository’s data [2]. Each image’s 64 pixels, from 0 to 16, are divided by 16 so that they run from 0 to 1, and a random 1,200 images form a training set, with the other images as a test set.

title: Feedforward Networks
section: 2.1 Two layers with nothing between them
text:
2.1 Two layers with nothing between them






ExrExercise 1 (Two layers with nothing between them)






Exercise 1 (Two layers with nothing between them) A layer first = nn.Linear(64, 32) maps a digit’s 64 pixels \(\vx\) to 32 numbers \(\matr{W}_1 \vx + \vecf{b}_1\), and a layer second = nn.Linear(32, 10) maps 32 numbers \(\vecf{u}\) to 10 numbers \(\matr{W}_2 \vecf{u} + \vecf{b}_2\). What kind of function of \(\vx\) does the stack second(first(x)) compute?










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. Substituting the first layer into the second,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\matr{W}_2 \paren{\matr{W}_1 \vx + \vecf{b}_1} + \vecf{b}_2
&= \matr{W}_2 \matr{W}_1 \vx + \matr{W}_2 \vecf{b}_1 + \vecf{b}_2
&& \text{(distribute $\matr{W}_2$)} \\
&= \underbrace{\paren{\matr{W}_2 \matr{W}_1}}_{10 \times 64} \vx
+ \underbrace{\paren{\matr{W}_2 \vecf{b}_1 + \vecf{b}_2}}_{10 \times 1}
&& \text{(group the terms that do not involve $\vx$)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So the stack is an affine function of \(\vx\), the same kind of function as one nn.Linear(64, 10), with weight matrix \(\matr{W}_2 \matr{W}_1\) and bias \(\matr{W}_2 \vecf{b}_1 + \vecf{b}_2\). The 32 numbers in the middle add nothing that one layer could not compute.

Show codefirst = nn.Linear(64, 32)
second = nn.Linear(32, 10)
weight = second.weight @ first.weight
bias = second.weight @ first.bias + second.bias
stacked = second(first(x_test))
one_layer = x_test @ weight.T + bias
stack_gap = (stacked - one_layer).abs().max().item()
print(weight.shape, bias.shape, stack_gap)

torch.Size([10, 64]) torch.Size([10]) 1.4901161193847656e-07


On the 597 test images, the stack and the single layer agree to within 1.5e-07, a rounding error. nn.Linear stores \(\matr{W}\) with one row per output, and computes x @ weight.T + bias for a tensor x with one row per image.

title: Feedforward Networks
text:
2.2 A function between the layers






ExrExercise 2 (A function between the layers)






Exercise 2 (A function between the layers) Suppose the logistic function, \(\sigmoidf{z} = 1 / \paren{1 + \e{-z}}\), is applied to each of the 32 numbers between the two layers of Exercise 1, giving second(torch.sigmoid(first(x))). Is that stack still an affine function of \(\vx\)?






TipHint



An affine function \(f\) maps the midpoint of two inputs to the midpoint of their outputs: \(f\paren{\frac{1}{2}(\vx + \vx')} = \frac{1}{2}\paren{f(\vx) + f(\vx')}\). Try two digits.












SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. 

Show codedef midpoint_gap(f, a, b):
    # Largest gap between f at the midpoint and the midpoint of f.
    return (f((a + b) / 2) - (f(a) + f(b)) / 2).abs().max().item()

a, b = x_test[0], x_test[1]
gap_linear = midpoint_gap(lambda v: second(first(v)), a, b)
gap_logistic = midpoint_gap(lambda v: second(torch.sigmoid(first(v))), a, b)
mean_abs_pre = first(torch.stack([a, b])).abs().mean().item()
print(gap_linear, gap_logistic, mean_abs_pre)

5.960464477539063e-08 0.0003224015235900879 0.2633136212825775


No. Take the first two test images, which show the digits 2 and 8. For them, the stack with nothing between its layers maps their midpoint to the midpoint of their outputs, to within 6e-08, a rounding error. With \(\sigmoid\) between the layers it misses by up to 0.00032, far more than a rounding error, so it is not an affine function. Even so, \(\sigmoid\) bends the untrained stack only a little. The untrained first layer’s numbers for these two images have a mean absolute value of 0.26, and near 0, \(\sigmoid\) is close to its tangent line, \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{z}{4}\). Training can move the numbers to where \(\sigmoid\) bends.
The logistic function bends each of the 32 numbers, so each of the 10 outputs is an affine function of 32 bent features, not of the pixels. Training moves \(\matr{W}_1\) and \(\vecf{b}_1\) as well as \(\matr{W}_2\) and \(\vecf{b}_2\), so it chooses those features.










DefDefinition 1 (Hidden layer)






Definition 1 (Hidden layer) A hidden layer of a network is a vector that the network computes from its input on the way to its output, and that is neither the input nor the output [1, Ch. 6].
The training data give an input and a target output for each example, but no target for a hidden layer: training chooses the parameters that compute it. These notes write a hidden layer as \(\vhidval\).










ExmExample 1 (The 32 hidden values of one digit)






Example 1 (The 32 hidden values of one digit)  

Show codehidden = torch.sigmoid(first(x_test[0]))
print(hidden.shape)

torch.Size([32])

Show codeprint(hidden.detach().numpy().round(2))

[0.39 0.42 0.48 0.41 0.57 0.49 0.51 0.51 0.54 0.6  0.44 0.53 0.64 0.41
 0.44 0.63 0.61 0.41 0.43 0.56 0.49 0.54 0.56 0.56 0.46 0.42 0.59 0.46
 0.55 0.54 0.6  0.46]


In Solution 2, torch.sigmoid(first(x)) is a hidden layer of width 32. For the first test image it holds the 32 numbers printed, each between 0 and 1. .detach() drops the record that automatic differentiation keeps, so that NumPy can print the values.










DefDefinition 2 (Unit (neuron))






Definition 2 (Unit (neuron)) A unit, or neuron, is one entry of a hidden layer [1, Ch. 6]. The number of units in a hidden layer is its width.










ExmExample 2 (One unit of the digits network)






Example 2 (One unit of the digits network) The hidden layer of Example 1 has 32 units. For the first test image, unit 1 holds 0.39, the first number printed there.










DefDefinition 3 (Activation function (nonlinearity))






Definition 3 (Activation function (nonlinearity)) An activation function, or nonlinearity, is a fixed function \(g: \reals \to \reals\), not an affine function, that a network applies to each entry of an affine function of the layer before, so that a hidden layer is
\[
\vhidval = g\paren{\matr{W} \vx + \vecf{b}},
\]
with \(g\) applied entry by entry [1, Sec. 6.3].










ExmExample 3 (The logistic function as an activation function)






Example 3 (The logistic function as an activation function)  

Show codepre = first(x_test[0])
print(pre[:4].detach().numpy().round(3))

[-0.458 -0.31  -0.068 -0.356]

Show codeprint(torch.sigmoid(pre[:4]).detach().numpy().round(3))

[0.387 0.423 0.483 0.412]


In Example 1 the activation function is the logistic function, \(g(z) = \sigmoidf{z} = 1 / \paren{1 + \e{-z}}\). The first line printed holds the first 4 entries of \(\matr{W}_1 \vx + \vecf{b}_1\) for the first test image, and the second holds the logistic function of each. The logistic function maps each entry separately: entry 1 of the output depends only on entry 1 of the input.










DefDefinition 4 (Pre-activation)






Definition 4 (Pre-activation) The pre-activation of a hidden layer \(\vhidval = g\paren{\matr{W} \vx + \vecf{b}}\) is the vector \(\matr{W} \vx + \vecf{b}\) that goes into its activation function \(g\).










ExmExample 4 (The pre-activation of one digit)






Example 4 (The pre-activation of one digit) In Example 3, the first line printed holds the first 4 entries of the pre-activation of the hidden layer of Example 1, for the first test image, and the second line holds the same entries of the hidden layer itself.

title: Feedforward Networks
text:
2.3 Three activation functions






ExrExercise 3 (Three activation functions)






Exercise 3 (Three activation functions) How do the logistic function \(\sigmoidf{z}\), the hyperbolic tangent \(\tanhf{z}\), and the function \(\maxf{0, z}\) behave as \(\abs{z}\) grows large?










SolutionSolution 3






Solution 3. 

Show codez = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 401)
activations = {
    "logistic": torch.sigmoid(z),
    "tanh": torch.tanh(z),
    "max(0, z)": torch.relu(z),
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5), layout="constrained")
for name, value in activations.items():
    ax.plot(z, value, label=name);
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.5);
ax.set_xlabel("z");
ax.set_ylabel("g(z)");
ax.legend();
plt.show()









Large positive \(z\). \(\sigmoidf{z}\) levels off at 1, and \(\tanhf{z}\) levels off at 1, while \(\maxf{0, z} = z\) keeps growing.

Large negative \(z\). \(\sigmoidf{z}\) levels off at 0, and \(\tanhf{z}\) levels off at \(-1\), while \(\maxf{0, z}\) is exactly 0 for every negative \(z\).

\(\tanh\) is a rescaled logistic function, \(\tanhf{z} = 2 \sigmoidf{2z} - 1\), so its graph is the same S curve, centred on 0 instead of \(\frac{1}{2}\).










DefDefinition 5 (Rectified linear unit (ReLU))






Definition 5 (Rectified linear unit (ReLU)) The rectified linear unit, or ReLU, is the activation function
\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(z) = \maxf{0, z}
\]
[1, Sec. 6.3.1], [3]. PyTorch provides it as torch.relu and as the layer nn.ReLU(). In mathematics \(\maxf{0, z}\) is also called the positive part of \(z\), written \(z^+\). Deep Learning recommends ReLU as the default activation function for hidden layers [1, Sec. 6.1]. 










ExmExample 5 (ReLU on the digits)






Example 5 (ReLU on the digits)  

Show codehidden_relu = torch.relu(first(x_test))
zero_share = (hidden_relu == 0).float().mean().item()
print(hidden_relu.shape, zero_share)

torch.Size([597, 32]) 0.4586997628211975


Applying the ReLU to the pre-activations of the first layer of Exercise 1, for all 597 test images, gives a hidden layer of width 32 for each image. 46% of its entries are exactly 0, one for each negative pre-activation.










ExrExercise 4 (Where the slopes vanish)






Exercise 4 (Where the slopes vanish) Using automatic differentiation, find the values of \(z\) at which the derivative of each activation function of Exercise 3 is close to 0.










SolutionSolution 4






Solution 4. 

Show codez = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 401, requires_grad=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5), layout="constrained")
slopes = {}
for name, g in [("logistic", torch.sigmoid), ("tanh", torch.tanh), ("ReLU", torch.relu)]:
    (slope,) = torch.autograd.grad(g(z).sum(), z)
    slopes[name] = slope
    ax.plot(z.detach(), slope, label=name);
ax.set_xlabel("z");
ax.set_ylabel("g'(z)");
ax.legend();
plt.show()






Show codelargest_logistic_slope = slopes["logistic"].max().item()
logistic_slope_at_4 = slopes["logistic"][-1].item()


Each output of g(z) depends only on the matching entry of z, so the gradient of g(z).sum() holds the derivative \(g'(z)\) at each point.


Logistic. Its derivative peaks at 0.25 at \(z = 0\), and is close to 0 once \(\abs{z}\) is large: 0.018 at \(z = 4\).

tanh. Its derivative peaks at 1 at \(z = 0\) and is also close to 0 for large \(\abs{z}\).

ReLU. Its derivative is 1 for every positive \(z\) and exactly 0 for every negative \(z\). At \(z = 0\) it has no derivative; PyTorch uses 0 there.

A unit whose pre-activation sits where the derivative is near 0 is saturated: a small change in its weights barely changes its output, so the gradient that training follows is small too. The logistic function and \(\tanh\) saturate on both sides, and ReLU only on its negative side.

title: Feedforward Networks
text:
2.4 Feedforward networks






DefDefinition 6 (Feedforward network (multilayer perceptron, MLP))






Definition 6 (Feedforward network (multilayer perceptron, MLP)) A feedforward network, or multilayer perceptron (MLP), computes its output \(\vecf{\hy}\) from its input \(\vx\) through a sequence of \(K\) hidden layers,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vhidval^{(1)} &= g\paren{\matr{W}^{(1)} \vx + \vecf{b}^{(1)}}, \\
\vhidval^{(\layeridx)} &= g\paren{\matr{W}^{(\layeridx)} \vhidval^{(\layeridx - 1)} + \vecf{b}^{(\layeridx)}},
\qquad \layeridx = 2, \dots, K, \\
\vecf{\hy} &= \matr{W}^{(K + 1)} \vhidval^{(K)} + \vecf{b}^{(K + 1)},
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(g\) is an activation function and the weight matrices \(\matr{W}^{(\layeridx)}\) and bias vectors \(\vecf{b}^{(\layeridx)}\) are the network’s parameters [1, Ch. 6]. Information flows from the input to the output, with no path from a later layer back to an earlier one; “feedforward” names that.
Every layer of an MLP is fully connected, so it is also called a fully connected network, and Deep Learning calls it a deep feedforward network. It contains no perceptron in Rosenblatt’s sense, a threshold function of a weighted sum [4], so the name is historical. Its depth is \(K + 1\). The last layer has no activation function; how its numbers become predictions depends on the task.










ExmExample 6 (An MLP for the digits)






Example 6 (An MLP for the digits)  

Show code_ = torch.manual_seed(1)
mlp = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(64, 32),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(32, 10),
)
print(mlp)

Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=32, bias=True)
  (1): ReLU()
  (2): Linear(in_features=32, out_features=10, bias=True)
)

Show codescores = mlp(x_test[:5])
print(scores.shape)

torch.Size([5, 10])


nn.Sequential applies its layers in order, so mlp is a feedforward network with one hidden layer of width 32, the ReLU as its activation function, and 10 outputs, one per digit. For 5 test images it returns a tensor of shape (5, 10): 10 numbers for each image.










RemarkRemark 1 (Writing a layer)






Remark 1 (Writing a layer). One layer is written here as \(g\paren{\matr{W} \vx + \vecf{b}}\), with \(\vx\) a column vector and \(\matr{W}\) having one row per output. Other sources write it differently:

PyTorch’s nn.Linear stores \(\matr{W}\) in the same orientation, but takes a batch of inputs with one row per example, and computes x @ weight.T + bias.

Deep Learning writes \(g\paren{\tp{\matr{W}} \vx + \vecf{c}}\), with one column of \(\matr{W}\) per output [1, Sec. 6.1].

lds puts a 1 at the start of \(\vx\) and folds the bias into \(\matr{W}\).












ReadingRead





Deep Learning’s Chapter 6 covers feedforward networks, their output units and their activation functions [1, Ch. 6].

title: Feedforward Networks
text:
3.1 From scores to probabilities






ExrExercise 5 (From scores to probabilities)






Exercise 5 (From scores to probabilities) The MLP of Example 6 gives each image 10 real numbers, positive or negative. How can they become 10 probabilities, one per digit, each positive and adding up to 1?










SolutionSolution 5






Solution 5. Apply the softmax function: exponentiate each number, which makes it positive, then divide by the sum of the exponentials, which makes them add up to 1.

Show codeprobabilities = torch.softmax(scores, dim=1)
print(probabilities.detach().numpy().round(3))

[[0.094 0.092 0.106 0.102 0.141 0.098 0.083 0.104 0.099 0.081]
 [0.084 0.091 0.121 0.093 0.153 0.085 0.073 0.109 0.109 0.082]
 [0.094 0.084 0.121 0.097 0.142 0.089 0.082 0.098 0.113 0.08 ]
 [0.09  0.088 0.119 0.1   0.143 0.087 0.076 0.106 0.103 0.087]
 [0.09  0.088 0.129 0.1   0.144 0.084 0.075 0.108 0.105 0.075]]

Show codeprint(probabilities.sum(dim=1))

tensor([1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000], grad_fn=<SumBackward1>)


dim=1 applies softmax across the 10 numbers in each row, one row per image. Each row of probabilities adds up to 1, and each is near \(\frac{1}{10}\), since the network is untrained.










DefDefinition 7 (Logits)






Definition 7 (Logits) The logits of a classification network are the numbers its output layer computes for each class, before the softmax function turns them into probabilities. PyTorch’s documentation uses this name.
The name comes from the logit function, the log odds, but most logits are not log odds. Adding one number to every logit leaves the softmax unchanged, so only their differences matter: with two classes, the difference \(z_2 - z_1\) is the log odds of class 2. Other names for logits are scores and unnormalized log probabilities.










ExmExample 7 (Shifting the logits)






Example 7 (Shifting the logits)  

Show codelogits = mlp(x_test[:1])
shifted = logits + 5
softmax_gap = (torch.softmax(shifted, dim=1) - torch.softmax(logits, dim=1)).abs().max().item()
print(logits.detach().numpy().round(3))

[[ 0.    -0.024  0.112  0.08   0.404  0.04  -0.133  0.095  0.045 -0.158]]

Show codeprint(softmax_gap)

2.9802322387695312e-08


The logits of the first test image are the 10 numbers printed. Adding 5 to each changes the softmax probabilities by at most 3e-08, a rounding error.










ExrExercise 6 (The loss before training)






Exercise 6 (The loss before training) The untrained MLP of Example 6 gives each test image probabilities near \(\frac{1}{10}\). About what mean cross-entropy loss should it have on the test set?










SolutionSolution 6






Solution 6. The cross-entropy loss of one image is \(-\log\) of the probability the network gives its true class. If every probability is \(\frac{1}{10}\), every image’s loss is \(-\log \frac{1}{10} = \log 10\), and so is their mean.

Show codestart_loss = nn.functional.cross_entropy(mlp(x_test), y_test).item()
print(start_loss, np.log(10))

2.3070168495178223 2.302585092994046


nn.functional.cross_entropy takes the logits and the true digits, and returns the mean loss over the test set, 2.307, close to \(\log 10 \approx 2.303\). A training run whose first loss is far from \(\log C\), for \(C\) classes, is worth checking for a bug before it runs further.

title: Feedforward Networks
text:
3.2 Computing the loss from logits






ExrExercise 7 (Softmax straight from its formula)






Exercise 7 (Softmax straight from its formula) A trained network can be confident, with logits in the hundreds. Take z to be the first test image’s logits from Example 7 times 1,000. What goes wrong when the softmax of z is computed with its formula, torch.exp(z) / torch.exp(z).sum()?










SolutionSolution 7






Solution 7. 

Show codez = (1000 * logits[0]).detach()
naive = torch.exp(z) / torch.exp(z).sum()
largest_float = torch.finfo(torch.float32).max
print(z.numpy().round(1))

[ 4.000e-01 -2.380e+01  1.118e+02  7.990e+01  4.042e+02  3.990e+01
 -1.331e+02  9.520e+01  4.500e+01 -1.576e+02]

Show codeprint(naive)

tensor([0., 0., nan, 0., nan, 0., 0., nan, 0., 0.])

Show codeprint(np.log(largest_float))

88.72283905206835

Show coden_nan = torch.isnan(naive).sum().item()
n_zero = (naive == 0).sum().item()
print(n_nan, n_zero)

3 7


The result holds 3 nans and 7 zeros. A float32 number cannot be larger than about \(3.4 \times 10^{38}\), so torch.exp(z) is infinite for every \(z\) above the log of that number, about 88.7, and infinity divided by infinity is nan. Every other entry has a finite exponential divided by that infinite sum, so its probability is 0, and the log of 0 is \(-\infty\).










ExrExercise 8 (The log of a softmax probability)






Exercise 8 (The log of a softmax probability) The cross-entropy loss needs \(\log \operatorname{softmax}(\vz)_m\), not the probability itself. Write \(\log \operatorname{softmax}(\vz)_m\) without a fraction.










SolutionSolution 8






Solution 8. \[
\begin{aligned}
\log \operatorname{softmax}(\vz)_m
&= \log \frac{\e{z_m}}{\sumto{k}{C} \e{z_k}}
&& \text{(the softmax function)} \\
&= \log \e{z_m} - \log \sumto{k}{C} \e{z_k}
&& \text{(log of a quotient)} \\
&= z_m - \log \sumto{k}{C} \e{z_k}
&& \text{($\log$ undoes $\expt$)}
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term needs no exponential at all. Only the second, the log of a sum of exponentials, can still overflow.










DefDefinition 8 (Log-sum-exp)






Definition 8 (Log-sum-exp) The log-sum-exp function maps a vector \(\vz \in \reals^C\) to
\[
\operatorname{LSE}(\vz) = \log \sumto{k}{C} \e{z_k}
\]
[1, Sec. 6.2.2.3]. It is the log of the denominator of the softmax function. PyTorch provides it as torch.logsumexp. \(\operatorname{LSE}\) is differentiable. \(\operatorname{LSE}(\vz)\) is at least the largest entry of \(\vz\) and at most that entry plus \(\log C\). So it is called a smooth maximum.










ExmExample 8 (Log-sum-exp of the logits)






Example 8 (Log-sum-exp of the logits)  

Show codelse = torch.logsumexp(logits[0], dim=0).item()
largest_logit = logits[0].max().item()
print(lse, largest_logit, largest_logit + np.log(10))

2.360166072845459 0.4042101502418518 2.7067952432358977


For the first test image’s logits, \(\operatorname{LSE}\) is 2.360, between the largest logit, 0.404, and that logit plus \(\log 10\).










LemTheorem 1 (Log softmax)






Theorem 1 (Log softmax) For \(\vz \in \reals^C\) and \(m = 1, \dots, C\),
\[
\log \operatorname{softmax}(\vz)_m = z_m - \operatorname{LSE}(\vz).
\]










ProofProof






Proof. By Solution 8 and Definition 8.










ExmExample 9 (Log softmax of the logits)






Example 9 (Log softmax of the logits)  

Show codeby_theorem = logits[0] - torch.logsumexp(logits[0], dim=0)
by_torch = torch.log_softmax(logits[0], dim=0)
log_softmax_gap = (by_theorem - by_torch).abs().max().item()
print(by_theorem.detach().numpy().round(3))

[-2.36  -2.384 -2.248 -2.28  -1.956 -2.32  -2.493 -2.265 -2.315 -2.518]

Show codeprint(log_softmax_gap)

2.384185791015625e-07


For the first test image, the logits minus their log-sum-exp agree with PyTorch’s torch.log_softmax to within 2.4e-07. Each is near \(\log \frac{1}{10} \approx -2.30\).










ExrExercise 9 (Computing log-sum-exp without overflow)






Exercise 9 (Computing log-sum-exp without overflow) Let \(c\) be any number. Write \(\operatorname{LSE}(\vz)\) in terms of \(c\) and \(\operatorname{LSE}\) of the shifted vector \(\vz - c\), whose entries are \(z_k - c\).










SolutionSolution 9






Solution 9. \[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{LSE}(\vz)
&= \log \sumto{k}{C} \e{z_k}
&& \text{(definition of $\operatorname{LSE}$)} \\
&= \log \sumto{k}{C} \e{c} \e{z_k - c}
&& \text{(add and subtract $c$ in each exponent)} \\
&= \log \paren{\e{c} \sumto{k}{C} \e{z_k - c}}
&& \text{(take $\e{c}$ out of the sum)} \\
&= c + \log \sumto{k}{C} \e{z_k - c}
&& \text{(log of a product)} \\
&= c + \operatorname{LSE}(\vz - c)
&& \text{(definition of $\operatorname{LSE}$)}
\end{aligned}
\]










LemTheorem 2 (Shifting log-sum-exp)






Theorem 2 (Shifting log-sum-exp) For \(\vz \in \reals^C\) and any \(c \in \reals\),
\[
\operatorname{LSE}(\vz) = c + \operatorname{LSE}(\vz - c).
\]










ProofProof






Proof. By Solution 9.










ExrExercise 10 (Choosing the shift)






Exercise 10 (Choosing the shift) Which \(c\) in Theorem 2 keeps every exponential in \(\operatorname{LSE}(\vz - c)\) from overflowing?










SolutionSolution 10






Solution 10. Take \(c = \max_k z_k\). Then every exponent \(z_k - c\) is at most 0, so no exponential exceeds 1. One exponent is exactly 0, so the sum is at least 1, and its log is not \(-\infty\).










ExmExample 10 (The confident logits again)






Example 10 (The confident logits again)  

Show codec = z.max()
shifted_lse = (c + torch.log(torch.exp(z - c).sum())).item()
print(shifted_lse, torch.logsumexp(z, dim=0).item())

404.21014404296875 404.21014404296875

Show codeprint(torch.log_softmax(z, dim=0))

tensor([-403.7620, -428.0196, -292.4266, -324.3521,    0.0000, -364.2654,
        -537.2988, -308.9668, -359.2179, -561.8227])


For the logits times 1,000 of Solution 7, shifting by their largest entry gives \(\operatorname{LSE} = 404.2\), the same value torch.logsumexp returns, and torch.log_softmax gives finite log probabilities where the formula gave nan.










RemarkRemark 2 (Why PyTorch’s cross-entropy takes logits)






Remark 2 (Why PyTorch’s cross-entropy takes logits). nn.CrossEntropyLoss and nn.functional.cross_entropy take logits, not probabilities. They compute the log probabilities by Theorem 1, with the shift of Theorem 2, so the loss stays finite for any logits. A classification network built for them ends with a linear layer and no softmax: softmax is applied only when probabilities are wanted for their own sake, as in Solution 5. Putting nn.Softmax at the end of the network and then calling nn.CrossEntropyLoss applies softmax twice.

title: Feedforward Networks
text:
3.3 Other kinds of output






ExrExercise 11 (An output layer for two classes)






Exercise 11 (An output layer for two classes) An MLP is to tell 0s from 1s, predicting the probability that a digit is a 1. What should its output layer compute?










SolutionSolution 11






Solution 11. One number \(z\), the logit of a 1, turned into a probability by the logistic function, \(\sigmoidf{z}\). That is the soft 0-or-1 rule of the PyTorch chapter, with \(z\) computed by a network instead of from one feature.
Two outputs with softmax would also work, but they carry one number too many: \(\operatorname{softmax}(z_1, z_2)_2 = \sigmoidf{z_2 - z_1}\), so only the difference of the two logits matters.










ExrExercise 12 (A loss for two classes)






Exercise 12 (A loss for two classes) What loss should training minimize for the output layer of Solution 11?










SolutionSolution 12






Solution 12. Use the log loss, which is the cross-entropy loss for two classes. PyTorch’s nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss takes the logit \(z\) itself, for the reason of Remark 2.










ExrExercise 13 (An output layer for a number)






Exercise 13 (An output layer for a number) An MLP is to predict a car’s fuel economy in miles per gallon. What should its output layer compute?










SolutionSolution 13






Solution 13. One number, with no activation function: any real number can be a prediction, and squashing it with the logistic function or the ReLU would rule some out.










ExrExercise 14 (A loss for a number)






Exercise 14 (A loss for a number) What loss should training minimize for the output layer of Solution 13?










SolutionSolution 14






Solution 14. Use the mean squared error, PyTorch’s nn.MSELoss. Minimizing the mean squared error is maximum likelihood when the output is the mean of a normal distribution with a fixed variance [1, Sec. 6.2.2.1], just as the cross-entropy loss is maximum likelihood for the probabilities of the classes.










RemarkRemark 3 (Output layers and their losses)






Remark 3 (Output layers and their losses). Solution 5, Solution 11 and Solution 13 pair each kind of target with an output layer and a loss, each the negative log-likelihood of a distribution for the target [1, Sec. 6.2.2]:

title: Feedforward Networks
text:
4.1 Training the MLP






ExrExercise 15 (Training the MLP on the digits)






Exercise 15 (Training the MLP on the digits) Train the MLP of Example 6 on the 1,200 training images, with nn.CrossEntropyLoss, taking 500 steps of torch.optim.SGD with a learning rate of 0.5, each on the whole training set. What fraction of the test images does it classify correctly?










SolutionSolution 15






Solution 15. 

Show codeloss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(mlp.parameters(), lr=0.5)
for step in range(500):
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(mlp(x_train), y_train)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

with torch.no_grad():
    predicted = mlp(x_test).argmax(dim=1)
test_accuracy = (predicted == y_test).float().mean().item()
print(loss.item(), test_accuracy)

0.044963538646698 0.9698492288589478


The trained network classifies 97.0% of the 597 test images correctly, against 10% for guessing. The loop is the training step of the PyTorch chapter, and the predicted digit is the one with the largest logit, which is also the one with the largest softmax probability.

title: Feedforward Networks
text:
4.2 Bends in a ReLU network






ExrExercise 16 (The shape of a small ReLU network)






Exercise 16 (The shape of a small ReLU network) An MLP has one input \(z \in \reals\), one hidden layer of \(L\) ReLU units, and one output with no activation function:
\[
\hy = c + \sumto{i}{L} v_i \maxf{0, w_i z + b_i}.
\]
What does the graph of \(\hy\) against \(z\) look like?










SolutionSolution 16






Solution 16. For \(w_i \neq 0\), unit \(i\) is 0 on one side of \(z = -b_i / w_i\) and the line \(w_i z + b_i\) on the other, so its graph is two straight pieces that meet at that point. A weighted sum of such graphs, plus a constant, is still made of straight pieces. It can change slope only where some unit does. So the graph of \(\hy\) is a connected chain of straight pieces, with at most \(L\) bends.

Show code_ = torch.manual_seed(3)
tiny = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, 3), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(3, 1))
z = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 601).unsqueeze(1)
with torch.no_grad():
    y_hat = tiny(z)
    bends = (-tiny[0].bias / tiny[0].weight.squeeze()).numpy()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5), layout="constrained")
ax.plot(z, y_hat);
for bend in bends:
    ax.axvline(bend, color="gray", linestyle=":");
ax.set_xlabel("z");
ax.set_ylabel("network output");
plt.show()







For a random network with \(L = 3\), the dotted lines mark the three points \(-b_i / w_i\), and the graph bends at each one that lies in the plotted range.










ExrExercise 17 (Following any curve)






Exercise 17 (Following any curve) Let \(f\) be a continuous function on an interval \([a, b]\). Could a network like the one in Exercise 16 follow \(f\) as closely as you like?










SolutionSolution 17






Solution 17. Yes, with enough units. Mark points on the graph of \(f\) at closely spaced values of \(z\), and join neighbouring points with straight lines. Because \(f\) is continuous on a closed interval, it changes little between nearby points, so the joined-up graph stays as close to \(f\) as you like once the points are close enough together. Call the inner points \(t_1 < \dots < t_{n - 1}\), and the slopes of the \(n\) pieces \(s_1, \dots, s_n\). A network like the one in Exercise 16 draws the joined-up graph on \([a, b]\) with \(n\) units, one per piece, each with \(w_i = 1\):


\(c = f(a)\) starts the graph at the first point;
the unit \(s_1 \maxf{0, z - a}\) gives the first piece its slope;
for each inner point \(t_j\), the unit \(\paren{s_{j + 1} - s_j} \maxf{0, z - t_j}\) is 0 to the left of \(t_j\), and changes the slope from \(s_j\) to \(s_{j + 1}\) at \(t_j\).











LemTheorem 3 (Universal approximation)






Theorem 3 (Universal approximation) Let \(g\) be a continuous activation function that is not a polynomial, such as the logistic function or the ReLU. For every continuous function \(f\) on a closed and bounded set \(\mathcal{X} \subset \reals^{\inputdim}\) and every \(\epsilon > 0\), there is a width \(L\) and parameters \(\vw_i \in \reals^{\inputdim}\) and \(b_i, v_i, c \in \reals\) such that
\[
\abs{f(\vx) - \paren{c + \sumto{i}{L} v_i \, g\paren{\tp{\vw_i} \vx + b_i}}} < \epsilon
\quad \text{for every } \vx \in \mathcal{X}.
\]
[1, Sec. 6.4.1], [5].










ProofProof






Proof. For one input and the ReLU, Solution 17 gives the idea. Cybenko [6] proved the theorem for logistic-shaped activation functions, Hornik [7] for bounded nonconstant ones, and Leshno et al. [5] for every activation function that is not a polynomial; those proofs need more analysis than these notes assume.










ExmExample 11 (Universal approximation for one input)






Example 11 (Universal approximation for one input) For one input, the ReLU and a closed interval \([a, b]\), Solution 17 builds the network that Theorem 3 promises: it joins points on the graph of \(f\) with straight pieces, and gives the network one unit for each piece. Making the pieces shorter brings the network closer to \(f\), at the cost of more units.










ExrExercise 18 (Wider networks on the Auto data)






Exercise 18 (Wider networks on the Auto data) Fit networks with one hidden layer of ReLU units, of width 1, 3 and 20, to miles per gallon on horsepower in the Auto data. How does the training mean squared error change as the width grows?










SolutionSolution 18






Solution 18. 

Show codeauto = pd.read_csv("data/auto.csv")
hp = torch.tensor(auto["horsepower"].to_numpy(), dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)
mpg = torch.tensor(auto["mpg"].to_numpy(), dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)
hp_scaled = (hp - hp.mean()) / hp.std()
print(auto[["horsepower", "mpg"]].head(3))

   horsepower   mpg
0         130  18.0
1         165  15.0
2         150  18.0

Show coden_steps = 3000


def fit_width(width, steps=n_steps):
    # Fit a one-hidden-layer ReLU network of `width` units to mpg on horsepower.
    torch.manual_seed(2)
    net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(1, width), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(width, 1))
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.01)
    for step in range(steps):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(net(hp_scaled), mpg)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    return net, loss.item()


grid = torch.linspace(hp.min().item(), hp.max().item(), 300).unsqueeze(1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5), layout="constrained")
ax.scatter(hp, mpg, s=6, color="gray", alpha=0.6);
auto_mse = {}
for width in [1, 3, 20]:
    net, auto_mse[width] = fit_width(width)
    with torch.no_grad():
        ax.plot(grid, net((grid - hp.mean()) / hp.std()), label=f"width {width}");
ax.set_xlabel("horsepower");
ax.set_ylabel("mpg");
ax.legend();
plt.show()






Show codeprint(auto_mse)

{1: 19.619924545288086, 3: 18.540300369262695, 20: 18.385217666625977}


The Auto data hold 392 cars from the UCI Auto MPG dataset [8], from a local copy, data/auto.csv, of the version in lds. Each network fits miles per gallon on horsepower, rescaled to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, by 3,000 steps of gradient descent on the mean squared error. With 1 unit the fit can bend only once, and its training mean squared error is 19.6. With 3 units it is 18.5, and with 20 it is 18.4. So the error falls as the network gets wider. Theorem 3 says that a wide enough network can follow any continuous curve; it does not say that following the training data more closely predicts new cars better.










RemarkRemark 4 (What universal approximation leaves out)






Remark 4 (What universal approximation leaves out). Theorem 3 says that some network of one hidden layer comes within \(\epsilon\) of \(f\). It does not say how wide that network must be, a width that can grow very fast with the number of inputs \(\inputdim\), nor that training finds its parameters, nor that it predicts new data well [1, Sec. 6.4.1].
Depth helps with the first of these. A ReLU network’s graph is made of straight pieces, as Solution 16 showed for one input. For networks with the same total number of units, the number of pieces a deep network can make grows exponentially with its number of layers, while a network with one hidden layer makes far fewer [9]. Some functions with many pieces therefore need far fewer units in a network with several layers.

The exercises use the 1,797 digits of data/optdigits-test.csv [2], split as in the feedforward networks chapter, with 1,200 images in the training set. make_mlp() builds that chapter’s MLP, with the same starting weights each time, so that every method below starts from the same place.

title: Optimization
text:
2.1 Ten passes over the data






ExrExercise 1 (Ten passes over the data)






Exercise 1 (Ten passes over the data) Suppose one fresh MLP from make_mlp() is trained for 10 epochs of full-batch gradient descent with learning rate 0.5. Another is trained for 10 epochs of minibatch gradient descent with batch size 32 and learning rate 0.1. The minibatches of each pass come from a fresh shuffle of the training images, rather than being drawn with replacement. Which has the lower training loss after 10 epochs?










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. 

Show codedef train(mlp, optimizer, n_epochs, batch_size, scheduler=None, seed=0):
    # Minibatch training; returns the training loss after each epoch.
    shuffler = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    losses = []
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        shuffled = torch.randperm(n_train, generator=shuffler)
        for start in range(0, n_train, batch_size):
            batch = shuffled[start:start + batch_size]
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss_fn(mlp(x_train[batch]), y_train[batch]).backward()
            optimizer.step()
            if scheduler is not None:
                scheduler.step()
        with torch.no_grad():
            losses.append(loss_fn(mlp(x_train), y_train).item())
    return losses


full_mlp = make_mlp()
full_losses = train(full_mlp, torch.optim.SGD(full_mlp.parameters(), lr=0.5), 10, n_train)
mini_mlp = make_mlp()
mini_losses = train(mini_mlp, torch.optim.SGD(mini_mlp.parameters(), lr=0.1), 10, 32)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5), layout="constrained")
ax.plot(range(1, 11), full_losses, marker="o", label="full batch");
ax.plot(range(1, 11), mini_losses, marker="o", label="minibatches of 32");
ax.set_xlabel("epoch");
ax.set_ylabel("training loss");
ax.legend();
plt.show()







Minibatches win by far: after 10 epochs the training loss is 0.24 for minibatches of 32 and 1.95 for the full batch. An epoch costs about the same either way, since it computes the loss and its gradient once for each training image. Full-batch descent spends that cost on one step per epoch, while the minibatch version spends it on many smaller, noisier steps, each of which already points roughly downhill. batch_size=n_train makes train() take full-batch steps.

title: Optimization
section: 2.2 How noisy is a minibatch gradient?
text:
2.2 How noisy is a minibatch gradient?






ExrExercise 2 (How noisy is a minibatch gradient?)






Exercise 2 (How noisy is a minibatch gradient?) lds’s exercise on minibatches shows that, for minibatches drawn with replacement, the minibatch gradient’s variance is \(1/b\) times that of one image’s gradient, for batch size \(b\). For a fresh MLP at its starting parameters, and 200 minibatches each of sizes 8, 32 and 128, does \(b\) times the mean squared distance between the minibatch gradient and the full-batch gradient stay about the same?










SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. 

Show codenoise_mlp = make_mlp()


def flat_gradient(rows):
    # The loss gradient on the given training images, as one long vector.
    noise_mlp.zero_grad()
    loss_fn(noise_mlp(x_train[rows]), y_train[rows]).backward()
    return torch.cat([p.grad.flatten() for p in noise_mlp.parameters()])


full_gradient = flat_gradient(torch.arange(n_train))
sampler = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
noise = {}
for b in [8, 32, 128]:
    distances = []
    for draw in range(200):
        rows = torch.randint(n_train, (b,), generator=sampler)
        distances.append(((flat_gradient(rows) - full_gradient) ** 2).sum().item())
    noise[b] = np.mean(distances)
print({b: round(float(b * d), 2) for b, d in noise.items()})

{8: 4.55, 32: 4.6, 128: 4.44}


Yes. The mean squared distance falls from 0.569 at \(b = 8\) to 0.035 at \(b = 128\), and \(b\) times it stays between 4.4 and 4.6. The mean squared distance is the sum of the variances of the gradient’s entries, so it falls as \(1/b\), as each variance does. Quadrupling the batch size only halves the typical distance, which is one reason small batches are a good use of each gradient computation.

title: Optimization
text:
3.1 Momentum in PyTorch






RemarkRemark 1 (Momentum in PyTorch)






Remark 1 (Momentum in PyTorch). torch.optim.SGD(params, lr=alpha, momentum=beta) takes the steps of lds’s momentum, \(\vv_t = \beta \vv_{t - 1} + \vg_t\) and \(\vcoef_t = \vcoef_{t - 1} - \learnrate \vv_t\), where \(\vg_t\) is the gradient at step \(t\) and \(\vcoef_t\) the parameters after it. Its first step sets \(\vv_1 = \vg_1\), as \(\vv_0 = \vzero\) would [3]. Some sources scale the gradient term by \(1 - \beta\) or fold \(\learnrate\) into \(\vv_t\); the steps are the same up to a rescaled learning rate.

title: Optimization
text:
3.2 Momentum on a steady slope






ExrExercise 3 (Momentum on a steady slope)






Exercise 3 (Momentum on a steady slope) Suppose the gradient is the same vector \(\vg\) at every step, and momentum, updated as in Remark 1, starts from \(\vv_0 = \vzero\). What does the step \(\learnrate \vv_t\) approach as \(t\) grows?










SolutionSolution 3






Solution 3. Unrolling \(\vv_t = \beta \vv_{t - 1} + \vg\) from \(\vv_0 = \vzero\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\vv_t
&= \vg + \beta \vg + \dots + \beta^{t - 1} \vg
&& \text{(apply the update $t$ times)} \\
&= \frac{1 - \beta^t}{1 - \beta} \vg
&& \text{(sum of a geometric series, for $0 \le \beta < 1$)} \\
&\to \frac{1}{1 - \beta} \vg
&& \text{(since $\beta^t \to 0$)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So the step approaches \(\frac{\learnrate}{1 - \beta} \vg\): on a steady slope, momentum moves like plain gradient descent with learning rate \(\learnrate / (1 - \beta)\). With \(\beta = 0.9\), that learning rate is 10 times \(\learnrate\).

title: Optimization
Optimization
text:
3.4 Adam’s first step






ExrExercise 5 (Adam’s first step)






Exercise 5 (Adam’s first step) At Adam’s first step, one parameter has gradient \(g \neq 0\). Ignoring \(\smallconst\), how far does that step move the parameter?










SolutionSolution 5






Solution 5. With \(m_0 = u_0 = 0\), the first averages are \(m_1 = (1 - \beta_1) g\) and \(u_1 = (1 - \beta_2) g^2\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\est{m}_1}{\sqrt{\est{u}_1}}
&= \frac{m_1 / (1 - \beta_1)}{\sqrt{u_1 / (1 - \beta_2)}}
&& \text{(bias corrections at $t = 1$)} \\
&= \frac{g}{\sqrt{g^2}}
&& \text{(substitute $m_1$ and $u_1$)} \\
&= \frac{g}{\abs{g}}
&& \text{($\sqrt{g^2} = \abs{g}$)}
\end{aligned}
\]
So the first step moves the parameter by exactly \(\learnrate\), against the sign of \(g\), whatever the size of \(g\).

Show codew = torch.ones(2, requires_grad=True)
adam = torch.optim.Adam([w], lr=0.01)
w.grad = torch.tensor([1000.0, 0.001])
adam.step()
step = (1 - w.detach()).tolist()
print(step)

[0.009999990463256836, 0.009999871253967285]


Gradients of 1,000 and 0.001 move their parameters by 0.0100000 and 0.0099999, both close to the learning rate, 0.01. The small difference is the effect of \(\smallconst\). So the learning rate of Adam sets the size of each step on the parameters’ own scale. Later steps are also bounded by about the learning rate [4, Sec. 2.1]. A step of plain gradient descent is instead the learning rate times the gradient.

title: Optimization
text:
4.1 Starting slowly






DefDefinition 1 (Learning-rate warmup)






Definition 1 (Learning-rate warmup) Learning-rate warmup raises the learning rate from a small value to its target over the first steps of training, usually linearly, before the rest of the schedule takes over [5, Sec. 2.2]. With linear warmup over \(T_w\) steps to a target learning rate \(\learnrate\), step \(t = 0, 1, \dots, T_w - 1\) uses learning rate \(\learnrate (t + 1) / T_w\).










ExmExample 1 (Warmup to 0.1 over 100 steps)






Example 1 (Warmup to 0.1 over 100 steps)  

Show codetarget_rate, n_warmup_steps = 0.1, 100
warmup_rates = {t: target_rate * (t + 1) / n_warmup_steps for t in [0, 49, 99]}
print(warmup_rates)

{0: 0.001, 49: 0.05, 99: 0.1}


With \(T_w = 100\) and \(\learnrate = 0.1\), learning-rate warmup uses learning rate 0.001 at step 0, 0.05 at step 49, and 0.1 at step 99, the last step of the warmup.

title: Optimization
text:
4.2 A schedule in PyTorch






ExrExercise 6 (Warmup, then cosine decay)






Exercise 6 (Warmup, then cosine decay) A schedule for torch.optim.SGD at learning rate 0.1 uses learning-rate warmup over 100 steps, and then cosine decay to 0 at step 1,000. What learning rate does it give at step 550?










SolutionSolution 6






Solution 6. 

Show coden_warmup, n_steps = 100, 1000


def warmup_cosine(step):
    # The factor that multiplies the base learning rate at this step.
    if step < n_warmup:
        return (step + 1) / n_warmup
    progress = (step - n_warmup) / (n_steps - n_warmup)
    return 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * progress))


schedule_mlp = make_mlp()
sgd = torch.optim.SGD(schedule_mlp.parameters(), lr=0.1)
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(sgd, warmup_cosine)
rates = []
for step in range(n_steps):
    rates.append(sgd.param_groups[0]["lr"])
    sgd.step()
    scheduler.step()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5), layout="constrained")
ax.plot(rates);
ax.set_xlabel("step");
ax.set_ylabel("learning rate");
plt.show()






Show coderate_550 = rates[550]


0.050. Step 550 is halfway through the cosine part, from step 100 to step 1,000, and halfway there cosine decay gives half the base learning rate, since \(\frac{1}{2}\paren{1 + \cosf{\frac{\pi}{2}}} = \frac{1}{2}\). The loop calls scheduler.step() after sgd.step(), the order PyTorch expects, and train() in Solution 1 does the same at every minibatch. Here sgd.step() changes nothing, since no gradients have been computed; it is there only to show the order.










RemarkRemark 2 (Why warm up)






Remark 2 (Why warm up). At the start of training the parameters are far from good ones, and the gradients can be large, so a learning rate that works later can throw the network into a bad region in the first few steps. Goyal et al. [5] proposed gradual warmup for training with very large minibatches. For Adam, its running average of squared gradients rests on only a few gradients at first, so its step sizes vary widely, and warmup keeps those early steps small [6].

title: Optimization
section: 5.1 The scale of the starting weights
text:
5.1 The scale of the starting weights






ExrExercise 7 (How the starting scale grows or shrinks)






Exercise 7 (How the starting scale grows or shrinks) Suppose the training images are pushed through 10 layers, each computing \(\operatorname{ReLU}\paren{\matr{W} \vhidval}\) with width 256 and no bias. Every weight is drawn independently from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\). How does the standard deviation of the last layer’s values depend on \(\sigma\), for \(\sigma = 0.01\), for \(\sigma = \sqrt{2 / n_{\text{in}}}\), where \(n_{\text{in}}\) is the layer’s number of inputs, and for \(\sigma = 0.2\)?










SolutionSolution 7






Solution 7. 

Show codedef last_layer_sd(scale, depth=10, width=256):
    # scale(n_in) gives the standard deviation of the weights of a layer with n_in inputs.
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    h = x_train
    for layer in range(depth):
        n_in = h.shape[1]
        weight = scale(n_in) * torch.randn(width, n_in)
        h = torch.relu(h @ weight.T)
    return h.std().item()


init_sd = {
    "small": last_layer_sd(lambda n_in: 0.01),
    "he": last_layer_sd(lambda n_in: math.sqrt(2 / n_in)),
    "large": last_layer_sd(lambda n_in: 0.2),
    "pixels": x_train.std().item(),
}
print(init_sd)

{'small': 5.173762460120024e-11, 'he': 0.30115261673927307, 'large': 529.7935180664062, 'pixels': 0.37631645798683167}


The pixels have standard deviation 0.38. After 10 layers, \(\sigma = 0.01\) leaves values with standard deviation about \(10^{-10}\), \(\sigma = 0.2\) gives about \(10^{3}\), and \(\sigma = \sqrt{2 / n_{\text{in}}}\) gives 0.30, close to where it started. Each layer multiplies the typical size of the values by about \(\sigma \sqrt{n_{\text{in}} / 2}\): the weighted sum of \(n_{\text{in}}\) values has variance proportional to \(n_{\text{in}} \sigma^2\), and the ReLU zeroes about half of the results. That factor is 1 for \(\sigma^2 = 2 / n_{\text{in}}\), which is He initialization [7]. Since backpropagation multiplies by the same weight matrices on the way back, the gradients shrink or grow layer by layer in the same way.

title: Optimization
text:
5.2 PyTorch’s default






ExrExercise 8 (PyTorch’s starting weights)






Exercise 8 (PyTorch’s starting weights) nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) draws each weight independently and uniformly from the interval \(\paren{-1 / \sqrt{n_{\text{in}}}, 1 / \sqrt{n_{\text{in}}}}\) [8]. What is the variance of each weight?










SolutionSolution 8






Solution 8. A weight \(w\) drawn uniformly from \((-a, a)\) has mean 0, so its variance is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Var{w}
&= \E{w^2}
&& \text{(the mean is 0)} \\
&= \int_{-a}^{a} w^2 \frac{1}{2a} \, dw
&& \text{(the density is $\frac{1}{2a}$ on $(-a, a)$)} \\
&= \frac{1}{2a} \cdot \frac{2 a^3}{3}
&& \text{(integrate $w^2$ from $-a$ to $a$)} \\
&= \frac{a^2}{3},
\end{aligned}
\]
so with \(a = 1 / \sqrt{n_{\text{in}}}\) each weight has variance \(1 / (3 n_{\text{in}})\).

Show code_ = torch.manual_seed(0)
layer = nn.Linear(256, 256)
default_var_times_n = layer.weight.var().item() * 256
print(default_var_times_n)

0.33143436908721924


For nn.Linear(256, 256) the sample variance of the weights times 256 is 0.331, close to \(\frac{1}{3}\). This variance is \(\frac{1}{6}\) of He initialization’s \(2 / n_{\text{in}}\), so by Solution 7 each ReLU layer with PyTorch’s starting weights shrinks the values by a factor of about \(1 / \sqrt{6}\). nn.init.kaiming_normal_ gives a layer He initialization instead.

title: Optimization
section: 5.3 Starting every weight at the same value
text:
5.3 Starting every weight at the same value






ExrExercise 9 (Starting every weight at the same value)






Exercise 9 (Starting every weight at the same value) Suppose every weight and bias of a fresh MLP is set to 0.1. It is then trained for 5 epochs on minibatches of 32, with torch.optim.SGD at learning rate 0.1. What happens to the 32 units of its hidden layer?










SolutionSolution 9






Solution 9. 

Show codeconstant_mlp = make_mlp()
with torch.no_grad():
    for p in constant_mlp.parameters():
        _ = p.fill_(0.1)
_ = train(constant_mlp, torch.optim.SGD(constant_mlp.parameters(), lr=0.1), 5, 32)
first_weights = constant_mlp[0].weight
largest_row_gap = (first_weights - first_weights[0]).abs().max().item()
with torch.no_grad():
    constant_acc = (constant_mlp(x_test).argmax(dim=1) == y_test).float().mean().item()
print(largest_row_gap, constant_acc)

0.0 0.09380234777927399


They stay identical: after training, the largest difference between any row of the first layer’s weight matrix and the first row is 0, so all 32 units compute the same function of the pixels, and the network classifies only 9.4% of the test images correctly. Units that start equal receive equal gradients, since each enters the output in the same way, so every step changes them equally. The network has, in effect, one hidden unit.










RemarkRemark 3 (Random starting weights break the symmetry)






Remark 3 (Random starting weights break the symmetry). Drawing the starting weights at random makes each unit start as a different function, so the units receive different gradients and can come to compute different functions [1, Sec. 8.4]. The biases can start at 0, since the random weights already tell the units apart. Solution 7 and Solution 8 show how to choose the scale of the random weights.

text:
5.4 Further reading







ReadingRead





Deep Learning’s Chapter 8 covers minibatches, momentum, Adam and starting weights for deep networks [1, Ch. 8].

title: Normalization and residual connections
text:
1.1 Plan for this lecture
The backpropagation chapter found that the gradient of a deep MLP can shrink layer by layer, and the optimization chapter chose starting weights to keep each layer’s values at a steady size. This lecture tries two more ways to train a network of 20 such layers:

rescaling each layer’s values during training, across the images of a minibatch or across the units of one image;
adding each layer’s input to its output.

title: Normalization and residual connections
section: 1.2 The digits and a deep network
text:
1.2 The digits and a deep network

Show codeimport numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from torch import nn

_ = torch.manual_seed(481)
digits = pd.read_csv("data/optdigits-test.csv", header=None)
x = torch.tensor(digits.iloc[:, :64].to_numpy(), dtype=torch.float32) / 16
y = torch.tensor(digits[64].to_numpy())
n_train = 1200
order = torch.randperm(len(x))
x_train, y_train = x[order[:n_train]], y[order[:n_train]]
x_test, y_test = x[order[n_train:]], y[order[n_train:]]
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()


class Block(nn.Module):
    # One hidden layer of `width` ReLU units.
    # make_norm(width) builds a layer applied to its pre-activations;
    # nn.Identity leaves them unchanged.

    def __init__(self, width, make_norm=nn.Identity, residual=False):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(width, width)
        self.norm = make_norm(width)
        self.residual = residual

    def forward(self, h):
        out = torch.relu(self.norm(self.linear(h)))
        if self.residual:
            return h + out
        return out


def make_deep(make_norm=nn.Identity, residual=False, depth=20, width=64, seed=1):
    # A first layer from the 64 pixels, `depth` blocks, then 10 logits.
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    blocks = [Block(width, make_norm, residual) for _ in range(depth)]
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(64, width), nn.ReLU(), *blocks, nn.Linear(width, 10))


def train(net, n_epochs=5, lr=0.01, batch_size=32, seed=0):
    # Minibatch SGD; returns the training loss and the test accuracy at the end.
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=lr)
    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        net.train()
        shuffled = torch.randperm(n_train, generator=generator)
        for start in range(0, n_train, batch_size):
            batch = shuffled[start:start + batch_size]
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss_fn(net(x_train[batch]), y_train[batch]).backward()
            optimizer.step()
    net.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        train_loss = loss_fn(net(x_train), y_train).item()
        test_acc = (net(x_test).argmax(dim=1) == y_test).float().mean().item()
    return train_loss, test_acc


def first_layer_grad(net):
    # Size of the loss gradient for the first layer's weights, on 256 training images.
    net.train()
    net.zero_grad()
    loss_fn(net(x_train[:256]), y_train[:256]).backward()
    return net[0].weight.grad.norm().item()


def last_block_std(net):
    # Standard deviation of the last block's output, on 256 training images.
    net.train()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return net[:-1](x_train[:256]).std().item()

title: Normalization and residual connections
text:
3.1 Definition






DefDefinition 1 (Batch normalization)






Definition 1 (Batch normalization) Batch normalization rescales each pre-activation of a layer across the examples of a minibatch. For a minibatch of \(B\) examples, let \(z_{ij}\) be pre-activation \(j\) for example \(i\), with mean and variance over the minibatch
\[
\mu_j = \frac{1}{B} \sumto{i}{B} z_{ij},
\qquad
\sigma_j^2 = \frac{1}{B} \sumto{i}{B} \paren{z_{ij} - \mu_j}^2.
\]
Batch normalization replaces \(z_{ij}\) with
\[
\gamma_j \frac{z_{ij} - \mu_j}{\sqrt{\sigma_j^2 + \smallconst}} + \beta_j,
\]
where \(\gamma_j\) and \(\beta_j\) are parameters learned with the rest and \(\smallconst\) is a small constant that keeps the division finite [1], [2, Sec. 8.7.1]. When the network makes predictions, running averages of \(\mu_j\) and \(\sigma_j^2\) from training take the place of the minibatch’s. PyTorch’s running average of the variance divides by \(B - 1\) instead of \(B\) [3].










ExmExample 1 (nn.BatchNorm1d on a minibatch)






Example 1 (nn.BatchNorm1d on a minibatch)  

Show codebatch_norm = nn.BatchNorm1d(64)
pre = nn.Linear(64, 64)(x_train[:32]).detach()
normed = batch_norm(pre).detach()
print(pre.mean(dim=0)[:4], pre.std(dim=0, correction=0)[:4])

tensor([ 0.1275, -0.3611,  0.5323,  0.4476]) tensor([0.1708, 0.1277, 0.1898, 0.1267])

Show codeprint(normed.mean(dim=0)[:4], normed.std(dim=0, correction=0)[:4])

tensor([6.7055e-08, 2.5332e-07, 4.4703e-08, 1.8626e-07]) tensor([0.9998, 0.9997, 0.9999, 0.9997])

Show codelargest_mean = normed.mean(dim=0).abs().max().item()

std_max = normed.std(dim=0, correction=0).max().item()


nn.BatchNorm1d(64) applies batch normalization to 64 pre-activations. It starts with every \(\gamma_j = 1\) and every \(\beta_j = 0\) [3]. For 32 training images, the first 4 pre-activations of a random layer have the means and standard deviations on the first line. After batch normalization, on the second line, no column’s mean is farther from 0 than 3.3e-07, and the standard deviations run from 0.999 to 1.000.

ExrExercise 2 (Predicting for one image)






Exercise 2 (Predicting for one image) Why can batch normalization not use the mean and variance of the minibatch when a network makes a prediction for a single image?










SolutionSolution 2






Solution 2. A minibatch of one image has \(\mu_j = z_{1j}\) and \(\sigma_j^2 = 0\), so every normalized pre-activation would be 0, whatever the image. The prediction would not depend on the image at all.

torch.Size([1, 64])


nn.BatchNorm1d treats a minibatch of one differently in its two modes:


Training mode. It refuses the minibatch: “Expected more than 1 value per channel when training, got input size torch.Size([1, 64])”.

Evaluation mode. It uses its running averages instead, so it accepts a single image.

Evaluation mode is what makes predictions use the running averages. That is why train() calls net.eval() before it computes the test accuracy.

title: Normalization and residual connections
text:
4.1 Definition






DefDefinition 2 (Layer normalization)






Definition 2 (Layer normalization) Layer normalization rescales the pre-activations of a layer across the units of one example. For an example with pre-activations \(z_1, \dots, z_L\), it uses their mean and variance
\[
\mu = \frac{1}{L} \sumto{j}{L} z_j,
\qquad
\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{L} \sumto{j}{L} \paren{z_j - \mu}^2,
\]
and replaces each \(z_j\) with \(\gamma_j \paren{z_j - \mu} / \sqrt{\sigma^2 + \smallconst} + \beta_j\) [4]. It does the same in training and in prediction, since it never looks at other examples.










ExmExample 2 (nn.LayerNorm on one image)






Example 2 (nn.LayerNorm on one image)  

Show codelayer_norm = nn.LayerNorm(64)
row_normed = layer_norm(pre[:1]).detach()
print(row_normed.mean().item(), row_normed.std(correction=0).item())

-2.0489096641540527e-08 0.9999433159828186


nn.LayerNorm(64) applies layer normalization to each row of its input [5]. For the first training image alone, its 64 outputs have mean -2.0e-08 and standard deviation 1.000.

Because layer normalization never uses other examples, it also works for a minibatch of one and for sequences of different lengths [4].

title: Normalization and residual connections
text:
5.1 A residual block






RemarkRemark 1 (Residual connections in Block)






Remark 1 (Residual connections in Block). Block(width, residual=True) returns \(\vhidval + \operatorname{ReLU}\paren{\matr{W} \vhidval + \vecf{b}}\) for its input \(\vhidval\), a residual connection around one hidden layer. This block is simpler than those of He et al. [6], which go around two or three convolutional layers and apply the ReLU after the sum. The input and output have the same width, 64, so the sum is defined.

title: Normalization and residual connections
text:
5.2 Gradients with residual connections






ExrExercise 5 (The gradient through residual connections)






Exercise 5 (The gradient through residual connections) How large is the gradient at the first layer of make_deep(residual=True), compared with make_deep()?










SolutionSolution 5






Solution 5. 

Show coderesidual_grad = first_layer_grad(make_deep(residual=True))
print(residual_grad, plain_grad)

25.32086181640625 1.927740855833804e-09


The gradient has size 2.5e+01, against 1.9e-09 without residual connections. A block computes \(\vhidval + f(\vhidval)\), with \(f(\vhidval) = \operatorname{ReLU}\paren{\matr{W} \vhidval + \vecf{b}}\) from Remark 1, so its derivative with respect to \(\vhidval\) is the identity matrix plus the derivative of \(f\). Going back through a block, the gradient keeps a copy of itself through the identity. It keeps that copy however small the derivative of \(f\) is. Without the residual connection, the gradient passes only through the derivative of \(f\), and shrinks when that derivative is small. Across 20 blocks these derivatives multiply. So when each factor is below 1 in size, the gradient shrinks geometrically.

1.2 The digits as sequences

Show codeimport math

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import torch
from torch import nn

_ = torch.manual_seed(481)
digits = pd.read_csv("data/optdigits-test.csv", header=None)
pixels = torch.tensor(digits.iloc[:, :64].to_numpy(), dtype=torch.float32) / 16
y = torch.tensor(digits[64].to_numpy())
n_train = 1200
order = torch.randperm(len(pixels))
x_train, y_train = pixels[order[:n_train]], y[order[:n_train]]
x_test, y_test = pixels[order[n_train:]], y[order[n_train:]]
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
LR = 0.01
BATCH_SIZE = 32


class Reader(nn.Module):
    # Reads each image as a sequence of `step_size` pixels at a time,
    # with the recurrent layer `layer`, and classifies it from the last state.

    def __init__(self, layer, step_size, hidden_size=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.step_size = step_size
        self.recurrent = layer(step_size, hidden_size, batch_first=True)
        self.out = nn.Linear(hidden_size, 10)

    def forward(self, images):
        sequence = images.reshape(len(images), -1, self.step_size)
        states, _ = self.recurrent(sequence)
        return self.out(states[:, -1])


def make_reader(layer, step_size, seed=1):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    return Reader(layer, step_size)


def train(net, n_epochs=10, lr=LR, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, seed=0, max_norm=math.inf):
    # Adam on the training digits; returns the gradient norm before each step.
    # A finite `max_norm` rescales any larger gradient to that norm.
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=lr)
    generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    norms = []
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        net.train()
        shuffled = torch.randperm(n_train, generator=generator)
        for start in range(0, n_train, batch_size):
            batch = shuffled[start:start + batch_size]
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss_fn(net(x_train[batch]), y_train[batch]).backward()
            norm = nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(net.parameters(), max_norm)
            norms.append(norm.item())
            optimizer.step()
    return norms


def accuracy(net):
    # Fraction of the test digits that `net` classifies correctly.
    net.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return (net(x_test).argmax(dim=1) == y_test).float().mean().item()


print(make_reader(nn.RNN, 8))

Reader(
  (recurrent): RNN(8, 32, batch_first=True)
  (out): Linear(in_features=32, out_features=10, bias=True)
)


The exercises use the UCI optical digits [1], split as in the feedforward networks chapter, with 1,200 training images. Reader reads each image as a sequence, step_size pixels at a time, and classifies it with a linear layer on the last hidden state. With step_size=8, each step reads one row of the image. train() runs Adam with learning rate 0.01 and batch size 32.

Exercise 1 (What nn.RNN returns) nn.RNN(8, 32, batch_first=True) is a recurrent layer with inputs of length 8 and a hidden state of length 32. It returns two tensors. What are their shapes for the first 16 training digits, each read as a sequence of 8 rows?










SolutionSolution 1






Solution 1. 

Show coderecurrent = nn.RNN(8, 32, batch_first=True)
rows = x_train[:16].reshape(16, 8, 8)
states, last_state = recurrent(rows)

torch.Size([16, 8, 8]) torch.Size([16, 8, 32]) torch.Size([1, 16, 32]) True


With batch_first=True, the input has shape \(16 \times 8 \times 8\): 16 sequences of 8 steps, each step a row of 8 pixels. The first output holds the hidden state after every step, with shape \(16 \times 8 \times 32\). The second holds the hidden state after the last step only, with shape \(1 \times 16 \times 32\). Its first dimension counts stacked layers times directions, here 1 layer read in 1 direction [2]. Its entries equal the last step of the first output. Without batch_first=True, PyTorch expects the steps first and the sequences second.

title: Recurrent networks
text:
4.2 Two gates instead of three






DefDefinition 1 (Gated recurrent unit (GRU))






Definition 1 (Gated recurrent unit (GRU)) A gated recurrent unit (GRU) layer keeps only a hidden state \(\vhidval_t \in \reals^{H}\), with no separate cell state, and two gates [5]. In the form PyTorch computes [6],
\[\begin{aligned}
\vecf{z}_t &= \sigmoidf{\matr{W}_z \vx_t + \matr{U}_z \vhidval_{t-1} + \vecf{b}_z}, &&\text{(update gate)} \\
\vecf{r}_t &= \sigmoidf{\matr{W}_r \vx_t + \matr{U}_r \vhidval_{t-1} + \vecf{b}_r}, &&\text{(reset gate)} \\
\vecf{u}_t &= \tanhf{\matr{W}_u \vx_t + \vecf{b}_u + \vecf{r}_t \odot \paren{\matr{U}_u \vhidval_{t-1} + \vecf{c}_u}}, &&\text{(candidate)} \\
\vhidval_t &= \vecf{z}_t \odot \vhidval_{t-1} + \paren{1 - \vecf{z}_t} \odot \vecf{u}_t.
\end{aligned}\]
Here \(\vecf{c}_u\) is a second bias vector, and PyTorch also adds one to \(\matr{U}_z \vhidval_{t-1}\) and to \(\matr{U}_r \vhidval_{t-1}\). Cho et al. [5] apply the reset gate before the matrix, writing \(\matr{U}_u \paren{\vecf{r}_t \odot \vhidval_{t-1}}\) in the candidate, and also put \(\vecf{z}_t\) on the old state. Chung et al. [7] and the DATA 471 notes put \(1 - \vecf{z}_t\) on the old state instead, which swaps the meaning of \(\vecf{z}_t\) near 0 and near 1.










ExmExample 1 (Parameters of nn.GRU and nn.LSTM)






Example 1 (Parameters of nn.GRU and nn.LSTM)  

Show codedef n_params(net):
    return sum(p.numel() for p in net.parameters())


gru_count = n_params(nn.GRU(1, 32))
lstm_count = n_params(nn.LSTM(1, 32))
print(gru_count, lstm_count)

3360 4480


A GRU layer has three blocks of weights, for \(\vecf{z}_t\), \(\vecf{r}_t\) and \(\vecf{u}_t\), where an LSTM layer has four. PyTorch gives each block two bias vectors, one added to \(\matr{W} \vx_t\) and one to \(\matr{U} \vhidval_{t-1}\) [6]. So nn.GRU(1, 32) has \(3 \times 32 \times (1 + 32 + 2) = 3360\) parameters, and nn.LSTM(1, 32) has \(4 \times 32 \times (1 + 32 + 2) = 4480\).

84.4%



The GRU reader classifies 84.4% of the test digits correctly, 2.3 percentage points above the LSTM reader, with 75% as many parameters in its recurrent layer. So yes: the two readers differ by 14 of the 597 test digits. Both gated readers beat the plain recurrent readers. On other tasks, Chung et al. [7] found neither gated layer consistently better than the other.

title: Recurrent networks
section: 5.1 A one-hot vector times a matrix
text:
5.1 A one-hot vector times a matrix






ExrExercise 8 (Multiplying a one-hot vector by a matrix)






Exercise 8 (Multiplying a one-hot vector by a matrix) A network that reads text needs each character as a vector. Number the 26 lowercase letters and the space from 0 to 26, so "c" is 2. Count vector entries and matrix rows from 0 as well. Let \(\vecf{e}_2 \in \{0, 1\}^{27}\) be the one-hot encoding of "c", and let \(\matr{E}\) be the \(27 \times 4\) matrix printed below. What is \(\tp{\vecf{e}_2} \matr{E}\)?

Show codealphabet = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz "
_ = torch.manual_seed(2)
E = torch.randn(len(alphabet), 4).round(decimals=2)
print(E[:4])

tensor([[-1.0400,  0.9200, -1.3000, -1.1100],
        [-1.2200,  1.1700, -1.0600, -0.1200],
        [-0.9100,  0.3500, -0.5700, -0.2400],
        [ 1.0100, -0.7500, -0.2200, -0.4300]])












SolutionSolution 8






Solution 8. 

Show codeone_hot_c = nn.functional.one_hot(torch.tensor(alphabet.index("c")), len(alphabet)).float()
product = one_hot_c @ E
print(product, E[2], torch.equal(product, E[2]))

tensor([-0.9100,  0.3500, -0.5700, -0.2400]) tensor([-0.9100,  0.3500, -0.5700, -0.2400]) True


Entry \(j\) of \(\tp{\vecf{e}_2} \matr{E}\) is \(\sum_i (\vecf{e}_2)_i \matr{E}_{ij} = \matr{E}_{2j}\), since \((\vecf{e}_2)_i\) is 1 for \(i = 2\) and 0 for every other \(i\). So the product is row 2 of \(\matr{E}\), the third row printed above. Multiplying by a one-hot encoding only looks up a row. A network can skip multiplying by the 26 zeros and read the row directly.










DefDefinition 2 (Embedding layer)






Definition 2 (Embedding layer) An embedding layer maps each of \(K\) symbols, such as characters or words, to a vector in \(\reals^d\). Symbol \(k\) maps to row \(k\) of a \(K \times d\) matrix \(\matr{E}\) of parameters, learned with the rest of the network [4, Sec. 12.4.2]. Row \(k\) is the vector that represents symbol \(k\). The layer equals a linear layer with no bias applied to the one-hot encoding of the symbol, computed by looking up the row.










ExmExample 2 (nn.Embedding)






Example 2 (nn.Embedding)  

Show codeembed = nn.Embedding(len(alphabet), 4)
word = torch.tensor([alphabet.index(ch) for ch in "deep"])
vectors = embed(word)
same_rows = torch.equal(vectors, embed.weight[word])
print(word, vectors.shape, same_rows)

tensor([ 3,  4,  4, 15]) torch.Size([4, 4]) True


nn.Embedding(27, 4) is an embedding layer for the 27 characters, with a \(27 \times 4\) matrix weight [8]. It takes a tensor of whole-number indices, here the indices of the letters of "deep", and returns one row of weight for each. For the 4 letters the result has shape \(4 \times 4\). The two "e"s get the same vector. The returned rows equal the rows of embed.weight at those indices.
